bio.en: Julia Schottenstein is a product leader at dbt Labs, where she leads the dbt Cloud product, and previously held product roles at Facebook and Neural Magic.
bio.zh: 茱莉亚·舍滕施泰因（Julia Schottenstein）是 dbt Labs 的产品负责人，领导 dbt Cloud 产品，此前曾在 Facebook 和 Neural Magic 担任产品职务。

summary.en: Julia reframes M&A as the disciplined practice of creating "plan Bs" so you always have optionality with potential buyers. She advises founders to become strategically unavoidable to a small set of buyers by leaning into a genuine competitive advantage without burning bridges. The episode offers a pragmatic playbook for early M&A thinking.
summary.zh: 茱莉亚把并购重新定义为一种有纪律的"准备 B 计划"的实践，让你始终对潜在收购方保有选择权。她建议创始人，通过发挥真正的竞争优势、又不伤和气地切入，使自己在少数几个买家眼中变得"难以忽视"。本期提供了一份务实的早期并购思路与打法。

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: M&A is always about creating plan Bs. And the way I would think about it is for any one company, there's only ever two to three buyers that find what you're building to be extremely strategic. And the strategy that I would do in how do you get noticed is I would figure out the area that you bring a competitive advantage. And I would inflict pain on that potential buyer. Make it impossible for them to not notice you because that's when they're going to have their ears perk up and say, "Well, what's going on with this company?" (00:00:33): The really important piece here is you want to do that in a way that's still friendly and open. I see a lot of founders get this wrong and they prematurely will shut down a conversation or they won't talk to an incumbent or a potential future buyer because they take too competitive of a stance. But that's a mistake because M&A is all about creating plan Bs and you don't want to shut that door down prematurely because you don't know if you can really go the distance and be an independent company. So you want to have optionality.
turns.zh: 并购（M&A）始终关乎制定备用方案。在我看来，对于任何一家公司而言，只有两到三个买家会认为你所打造的业务具有极高的战略价值。那么如何吸引他们的注意呢？我的策略是明确你所在领域的竞争优势，并给潜在买家制造压力。让他们不得不注意到你，因为这时他们才会警觉起来，心想：“这家公司到底在搞什么？”（00:00:33）关键在于要保持沟通的友好和开放。我发现很多创始人会犯这样的错误——他们过早地终止对话，或者拒绝与现有企业或潜在买家沟通，因为他们采取了过于强硬的竞争姿态。但这其实是个错误，因为并购的核心在于制定备用方案。你不应过早关闭合作的大门，因为你无法预知是否能真正独立发展下去。因此，你需要保持灵活的选择权。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you have a really interesting career path in that you went from VC into product management. Usually it's the other way around. Usually PMs become VCs and it's right to see this version of it. So I wanted to start with just a question of just how did that come to be?
turns.zh: 你的职业发展路径确实很有趣——从风投转到产品管理。通常情况下，产品经理会转型成为风投，但以你这样的路径反过来确实少见。不过这种逆向发展倒也说得通。首先我想问，你是如何走上这条路的？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: I do have an unusual background, but it doesn't surprise me that people who are interested in product are also interested in investing and vice versa. For me, I've always had three interests broadly and that's an interest in business, an interest in technology and an interest in markets. And I get to express those interests both in investing and in product, but just with different weights. So in product you go a lot deeper on the tech and markets is less of a focus, but you still get to do all three. So I have a unusual background and I used to be a professional investor at NEA. Spent all my time investing in early stage startups that built for technical audiences. So think dev tools, infra data companies. (00:05:22): And in 2019 I first discovered dbt, which was an open source data transformation framework. And I got really very, very excited about dbt because when I talked to people that were using it, the way that they described their experience on dbt was like unlike anything I had heard before. It was much more of an identity for them than just a tool that they were using to get their job done. And that really struck me. And as I thought about what was happening in the market, there was a lot going on in 2019. The markets were changing quite a bit. Cloud data warehouses were starting to explode. This was the year where Snowflake went from a 4 billion company to a 12 billion company. And I thought to myself, if dbt worked, it could work in a really extraordinary way. And I naturally tried to spend all my time getting close to Tristan, who's the CEO and founder and I wanted to invest.
turns.zh: 我的背景确实比较特殊，但我并不惊讶对产品感兴趣的人同时也对投资感兴趣，反之亦然。对我而言，我一直有三个广泛的兴趣领域：商业、技术和市场。这些兴趣在投资和产品领域都能得以体现，只是侧重点不同。在产品领域，你需要更深入地钻研技术，而市场关注度较低，但这三个领域你都能有所涉猎。我在NEA曾是一名专业投资人，专注于为技术受众打造的初创企业。比如开发工具、基础设施数据公司等领域。（00:05:22）2019年，我首次接触到开源数据转换框架dbt。它让我兴奋不已，因为与我接触过的用户相比，他们对dbt的体验堪称非同寻常。它对他们的意义远不止是完成工作的工具，更像是一种身份认同。这让我深有感触。当时市场正经历巨大变革，云数据仓库开始兴起，Snowflake从40亿美元估值跃升至120亿美元。我当时想，如果dbt能成功，其影响力必将非同凡响。于是我开始主动接近dbt的CEO兼创始人Tristan，希望能参与投资。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So at this point you're a spec at NEA, you're trying to invest in dbt and okay, keep going.
turns.zh: 好的。那时你在NEA担任风投职位，正试图投资dbt，继续说下去。

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Yeah. So I was very, very excited. I thought if this worked, it could work in a really extraordinary way and I spent all my time trying to get Tristan to like me so that I could invest in the company. And then in 2020, I finally got the call that I was waiting for. Tristan said, "We're going to raise some money." He had a term sheet from a firm that he liked. It was a good venture fund, but he also liked me and he wanted to give me a shot and I was super excited to get that message because this is my chance. And unfortunately I ended up losing that deal to Sequoia. It's a formidable partner.
turns.zh: 是的。我非常兴奋，觉得如果成功了，其影响力必将非同凡响。我把所有时间都花在试图让Tristan喜欢我上，好能投资这家公司。2020年，我终于接到了期待已久的电话。Tristan说：“我们要融资了。”他拿到了心仪机构的投资意向书，是一家不错的风投基金，但他也看中了我，愿意给我一个机会。收到这个消息我超级激动，因为这就是我的机会。可惜最后输给了红杉资本，这个强劲对手。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Reasonable loss.
turns.zh: 合理的选择。

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: I was just so convicted that if was going to be a special company that I asked to even put my personal money in and I asked to put a very irresponsible, irrational amount, nearly like 20% of my liquid net worth into dbt because I was so convinced that this was special. And sometimes when deals don't work out as an investor, you can create this narrative in your head like, "Good, I dodged a bullet or better off without them or screw them." But for me that was quite the opposite with dbt. I really felt like dbt was this runaway train and it was special and I wanted to jump on board. So a few months later I ended up calling Tristan and asked him if I could be a part of the company that built the product that I thought was so special. So that was my unique path into product and to dbt.
turns.zh: 我当时深信，如果这家公司注定非同寻常，我甚至愿意投入个人资金——而且是一笔非常冒险、不理智的金额，接近我流动净资产的20%，因为我坚信它与众不同。作为投资者，当交易未能达成预期时，人们可能会在脑海中编织各种借口，比如“幸好躲过一劫”、“与他们分道扬镳反而更好”之类。但对我而言，DBT完全相反。我深切感受到DBT就像一列失控的列车，它极具独特性，我迫切想搭上这趟列车。几个月后，我最终致电特里斯坦，询问能否加入这家公司，共同打造我眼中极具革命性的产品。这便是我投身产品开发、加入DBT的独特机缘。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you invested in dbt and then an opportunity opened up where you ended up working there?
turns.zh: 所以你投资了DBT，然后后来又获得了在那里工作的机会？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: No, I think if I was able to invest I wouldn't be here. So I got no, the board ended up vetoing my personal investment, but it's okay because I ended up dedicating all of my personal time to building the company.
turns.zh: 不，我觉得如果我当时能够投资，恐怕就不会站在这里了。董事会否决了我的个人投资提议，不过没关系，因为我最终将全部精力投入到公司建设中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. So something you touched on there that was really interesting of what you saw about dbt that was so interesting and I think this is maybe a broader question of just in your time investing and finding a company like dbt early, what have you learned about just picking well, finding companies early especially? What are signs in your experience of just that this is going to be something really interesting that you might want to join? And this is more for people listening that are thinking about joining a company early on. What do you think they should look for?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，你刚才提到对DBT的独特洞察力非常有趣，我想这或许能引申出一个更广泛的问题——在投资过程中及早发现像DBT这样的公司，你学到了哪些关于精准选择、提前布局的经验？从你的经历来看，哪些迹象能预示这家公司将带来非凡机遇？特别是对于那些正考虑早期加入公司的听众，你认为他们应该关注哪些关键点？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: So the way I would look at joining an early stage company would be the same way I would evaluate investing in one. So there are four things that I care about when I'm looking at really early stage companies and it's people, market, product and distribution. And I'll touch on each of those four to say a little bit more about what specifically I'm looking at. So people, this is really the CEO, the founder of the company put simply do you trust this person to lead. And for me, Tristan had this really rare ability to paint a very compelling future of the industry and how dbt was going to be a part of making that vision a reality. But he also was really, really detailed in the day-to-day work of the analytics engineering work. And it was that range in scale that made me feel like this is a founder that's very rare and compelling. (00:09:42): The next is markets. We touched on it a little bit, but what I'm looking for in markets it's like is it growing? Is there space for new entrant to make its mark? And when it came to dbt, it was an explosive time in cloud data warehouses and it was that chaos that was really the opportunity for dbt because they created some orderliness and structure to the way that people worked with their data in the cloud data warehouse. So that was very compelling. The next is product. Everyone who's listening hopefully either is interested in products or has a product background. So I won't say too much there, but can you talk to users or potential customers, are they building something that's really special, unique? Can you hear that, spark that enthusiasm and figure out if this is going to be special. (00:10:31): And then the last, I think this is more important arguably than if they have a good product but is distribution, do they have an advantage on how are they going to get to market because that's really, really hard? And think about how they think about their competitive advantage on either the ecosystem or distribution and how they're going to ultimately sell the product. You're not going to get a 10 out of 10 on all four dimensions. So when you're joining a company, you also have the benefit of dedicating your time. So try to think if they're weaker on one dimension, what is it that you bring to the table or what are you special at that could potentially de-risk the success of the company
turns.zh:
因此，我看待加入一家早期阶段公司的方式，与评估投资一家公司的方法是一样的。在评估早期阶段公司时，我关注的四个关键点是：人、市场、产品和分销。接下来，我将分别探讨这四个方面，更深入地阐述我所关注的具体要点。

首先是人。说白了，就是公司的首席执行官和创始人。你是否信任这个人能领导好公司？就特里斯坦而言，他展现出非凡的能力，能描绘出行业令人振奋的未来图景，以及dbt如何助力实现这一愿景。但他在分析工程日常工作中也极其细致。这种兼顾宏观与微观的能力，让我深信他是一位极其难得且极具魅力的创始人。

（00:09:42）接下来是市场。我们之前略有提及，但我对市场的评估重点在于：市场是否在增长？是否有新进入者能崭露头角？以dbt为例，当时云数据仓库领域正处于爆发式增长期。正是这种混乱的局面，为dbt创造了机遇——他们为云数据仓库中的数据处理方式注入了秩序与结构。这实在令人心动。

（00:10:31）然后是产品。希望在座的每位听众要么对产品感兴趣，要么有产品背景。因此我不再赘述。但关键在于，你能否与用户或潜在客户交流？他们是否在打造真正独特、特别的产品？你能否激发他们的热情，并判断这是否会成为独树一帜的创新？

（00:11:03）最后一点，或许比拥有优秀产品更为重要的是分销。是否有进入市场的优势？毕竟这确实极具挑战性。思考他们如何在生态系统或分销方面建立竞争优势，以及如何最终将产品推向市场。四项维度不可能全满分。因此加入一家公司时，你还有专注时间的优势。若某一维度较弱，你能否贡献自己的专长或独特才能，从而降低公司的成功风险？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In terms of spark with a product. Right now on product market fit, now how do you know if you have product market fit? And a lot of it often comes down to there's a emotional reaction from someone you're talking to about the product you're building. There's like, "Holy shit, I want this now." Is there anything even more specific you've seen of just what is a sign that this, there's a spark that people are just really enthused? You talked about people made dbt part of their identity. Is there anything else there?
turns.zh: 关于产品市场契合度。目前如何判断是否具备产品市场契合度？这往往取决于与你交谈的人对正在开发的产品产生的情感反应。比如：“天哪，我现在就想要这个！” 你有没有更具体的例子，说明人们对产品的热情达到何种程度？你提到人们把dbt视为自身身份的一部分。还有其他迹象吗？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Yeah. It's can they not stop talking about it and that's the chatter about a product, they want to share it with their teammates or to other people at different companies. That just top of mind love and wanting to share what they've found with others is really a great sign that you're onto something. And then that spark will help do a lot of the work on how do you get to market because your evangelists are really your users of people that love what you're building.
turns.zh: 是的。比如他们忍不住谈论它，在产品圈子里分享。他们想把它介绍给团队成员或其他公司的同事。这种发自内心的喜爱和分享欲望，确实是产品成功的重要标志。这种热情将助力产品推向市场，因为这些传播者就是最忠实的用户，他们热爱你所打造的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What about in terms of the distribution bucket? What are some examples of just really important, I don't know, unique or effective distribution strategies or I don't know, unfair advantages you've seen maybe with dbt, maybe other companies? What are some examples of that?
turns.zh: 关于分销渠道方面呢？有没有一些非常重要、独特或有效的分销策略，或者说你见过的可能来自dbt、或者其他公司的那些不公平的优势？能举些例子吗？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: So dbt had an ecosystem advantage and they were open source and this helped really dramatically for lots of people to have low barrier friction to just try it out and spread organically. They first got started with very horizontal. People could just get started without ever even talking to sales and think that was a competitive advantage. But not all companies need to be product led. Some companies are enterprise top-down sales. So in those situations think about does the team really know how to land a complex enterprise sale? Do they have a background in that particular space? Do they have a network of connections? Can be different depending on what the company is selling, but you either want to see a company that's really strong at enterprise or really strong at the bottoms up.
turns.zh: dbt当时拥有生态系统优势，而且是开源的，这对很多人来说极大降低了试用门槛，帮助它实现了自然传播。他们最初采取的是横向推广策略。人们甚至无需与销售团队接触就能上手尝试，这可以视为一种竞争优势。但并非所有公司都需要以产品为导向。有些公司是自上而下的企业销售模式。在这种情况下，要考虑团队是否真正具备拿下复杂企业订单的能力？他们是否有相关领域的背景？是否拥有人脉资源？这会因所售产品类型而有所不同，但你要么看到一家在企业销售方面非常强大，或者在草根市场拓展方面非常出色的公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. So I want to shift a bit to talking about an area that you have a lot of experience in which a lot of people are also really interested in right now, which is M&A. I've invested in a lot of companies and maybe, I don't know, once a month I'm getting an email from a startup I've been investor in. There's just like, we're looking at maybe selling the company, things aren't working out the way we were hoping. And you've been on I think maybe all sides of the table of M&A transactions, including I think you led the acquisition of a company... I was an investor in the dbt acquired that I think is public company called Transform. So my question is just for founders who are currently thinking about M&A meaning acquisition essentially. What's your best advice for them for how to be most successful in M&A outcome for themselves?
turns.zh: 好的，不错。接下来我想转向你非常熟悉且当前备受关注的领域——并购。我投资过很多公司，可能每个月都会收到被投企业的邮件，内容大多是‘我们正考虑出售公司，业务进展不如预期’之类的。你应该参与过并购交易的各个环节，包括主导过收购案……我曾投资过dbt收购的公司，叫Transform，现已上市。所以我想问问那些正在考虑并购（尤其是收购）的创始人，对于如何在并购中取得最佳结果，你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: When it comes to acquisitions, the time to start thinking about an M&A strategy is hopefully when you don't need one. And the best strategy that I could give a founder is to have a really strong offense in building their company. And when founders start their businesses, they don't usually set out to start a company to sell it to another business. They start it to be an enduring independent standalone company. And if you have that path, then you'll have the upper hand in absolutely every single M&A conversation because you have a viable alternative, which is do nothing, stay the course, you don't have to sell. But of course that's not the case for most companies. Most companies don't have a viable path to being an independent company forever. So they have to think about M&A. So M&A is always about creating plan Bs. (00:14:49): And the way I would think about it is for any one company, there's only ever two to three buyers that find what you're building to be extremely strategic. And the strategy that I would do and how do you get noticed is I would figure out the area that you bring a competitive advantage and I would inflict pain on that potential buyer. Make it impossible for them to not notice you because that's when they're going to have their ears perk up and say, "Well, what's going on with this company?" We just bought this company Transform. They are playing a really good playbook here. (00:15:25): And the really important piece here is you want to do that in a way that's still friendly and open. I see a lot of founders get this wrong and they prematurely will shut down a conversation or they won't talk to an incumbent or a potential future buyer because they take too competitive of a stance. But that's a mistake because M&A is all about creating plan Bs and you don't want to shut that door down prematurely because you don't know if you can really go the distance and be an independent company. So you want to have optionality.
turns.zh:
谈到收购问题，最好是在你不需要制定并购策略的时候就开始思考它。而我能给创始人最好的建议，就是在构建公司时就采取强有力的进攻策略。大多数创业者创办公司时，初衷并非将其出售给其他企业，而是希望公司能持续独立发展。如果你能坚持这条道路，那么在任何并购谈判中你都将占据上风——因为你还有一个可行的替代方案：保持现有发展路线，拒绝出售。但显然大多数公司并非如此。多数公司并无永续独立的生存之道，所以不得不考虑并购策略。并购始终关乎制定后备计划。  
（00:14:49）我对此的看法是，任何公司只有两到三个买家会认为你的业务极具战略价值。我的策略是明确你的竞争优势所在，并对潜在买家制造压力，让他们不得不注意到你。这时他们才会竖起耳朵，问：“这家公司怎么回事？”比如我们刚收购的Transform公司，他们的策略就很成功。  
（00:15:25）关键在于要保持谈判的友好与开放。我发现许多创始人误解了这一点，过早终止谈判、拒绝与现有企业或潜在买家沟通，因为他们采取了过于竞争的姿态。但这是一个错误，因为并购的核心就是制定后备计划。你不应过早关闭这扇门，因为你无法预知公司能否真正独立发展。所以要保留选择权。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this term with pain on your potential acquirers. What are some examples of that? Who's done that well or what's an example of that interaction?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢你提到的“对潜在收购方制造压力”这个说法。能举些具体例子吗？有哪些公司在这方面做得很好，或者能举个具体的互动案例？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Yeah. I mean I can share the transform stories of a company we just acquired, we announced it in February. So dbt Labs, we build transformations, that's our main product. And we were venturing into a new product area that we call the semantic layer. And to describe what that is quickly, it's allowing companies to define their business metrics and so that whenever anyone queries it, we always serve back consistent data on those business metrics and transform. They were a pure play company only in this metrics layer, semantic layer. And they had a really strong product. (00:16:41): They had figured out some of the technical challenges and they had solved it early on. They had the benefit of having worked at Airbnb, which and Airbnb in the data world is famous for having a really successful semantic layer metrics layer called Minerva. And what we had at dbt Labs is really good distribution and ecosystem, but we were a little behind in bringing a product to market and we felt that pressure from Transform because they were doing such a great job at being vocal and loud about how their semantic layer solves these really hard technical problems. (00:17:20): But they didn't have any distribution. So that was really tough for them and they were putting pressure, but they were still positioning their company as a partner to us because they wanted our community to be excited about what they were building and hopefully lure them over to use their product. So because they had positioned themselves as a friendly partner when really we were trying to compete for this similar use case, when it came time to do an acquisition, we were really excited because we knew their product was good and they had already done a lot of the work to make integrating with dbt possible and that helps us post acquisition do the integration much more easily.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，我可以分享我们刚收购的一家公司的转型故事，我们在二月份宣布了这笔收购。DBT Labs专注于构建转换模型，这是我们的主营业务。当时我们正尝试进军一个新产品领域，称之为"语义层"。简单来说，这个产品能帮助企业定义业务指标，这样无论用户何时进行查询，我们都能始终提供一致的业务指标数据和转换结果。DBT Labs原本是一家专注于这一指标层和语义层的纯粹型公司，他们的产品实力非常强劲。（00:16:41）他们很早就攻克了技术难关，得益于曾在Airbnb工作的经验——Airbnb在数据领域以其成功的指标层和语义层产品Minerva闻名。DBT Labs拥有出色的产品分发和生态系统，但在产品上市方面稍显滞后。与此同时，Transform公司正大力宣传其语义层如何解决技术难题，这给我们带来了压力。（00:17:20）但Transform缺乏产品分发能力，这对他们来说是个挑战。尽管如此，他们仍将自己定位为我们的合作伙伴，希望借此吸引DBT的用户群体使用他们的产品。然而当我们试图在相似的应用场景中展开竞争时，收购DBT Labs的机会来临了。我们欣喜地发现，他们的产品质量上乘，已完成了与DBT集成的大部分工作，这极大地简化了收购后的整合过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you just think about either as a startup or even an incumbent about how to think about competition, how much emphasis, how much energy to put into thinking what competitors are doing and just how that informs your strategy?
turns.zh: 无论是初创企业还是传统巨头，如何看待竞争？应该投入多少精力去研究竞争对手的动态，以及这些信息如何指导自身战略？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: So we recently codified our philosophy when it comes to competition. And I'll give Nick Handel the founder of Transform who led this exercise at dbt Labs. But we really have three pillars when it comes to competition. So the first is hold true to our vision. We're really excited about the path and the journey that we're going on at dbt Labs and we don't want the distraction. So occasionally you'll have competitors maybe throw shade or throw stones, but most of that is just noise. If you have a lot of conviction that you're going in the right journey, you want to just keep your eyes straight ahead and run your best race and not be too distracted by what maybe some critics are saying. (00:19:00): The second philosophy we have is really a grow the pie philosophy. So we want to work with our partners in our ecosystem to make the opportunity set even larger and we see that today. We mostly serve reporting and BI use cases, we're seeing lots of companies start to operationalize their data. Now with this big wave of ML, clean Transform data assets are being used to train machine learning models so that the pie continues to grow. Let's focus on that as our target and work with people to make the opportunity set really attractive and not try to slice it up too thinly. (00:19:37): And then the last one is we want to lean into our strengths. So we have an ambition to be a platform company and we know what we're good at, but we also want to leave space for our ecosystem to offer solutions to our users that help them out. And we really want to foster an ecosystem where we can partner with lots of companies in the modern data stack. And generally speaking, when it comes to competition, we take a really long-term view and there are a few areas that we do want to hold our ground and that's in our transformation standard as well as our semantic standard because we believe those two are better served together for the user's sake. But for everything else, we really feel like we can work with our ecosystem and accomplish what we want to accomplish and also help them accomplish their goals too.
turns.zh:
最近，我们正式确立了关于竞争的核心理念。接下来，我将把这项工作的牵头者——Transform公司的创始人尼克·汉德尔（Nick Handel）介绍给大家。他在dbt Labs领导了这项工作。关于竞争，我们有三个核心原则。首先是坚守我们的愿景。我们对dbt Labs正在走的道路和未来充满激情，不想被外界干扰。偶尔会有竞争对手挑拨离间，但多数情况下这些噪音都无伤大雅。如果你坚信自己走在正确的道路上，就要专注前行，专注于自己的最佳表现，而不必理会某些批评者的言论。（00:19:00）  
第二个原则是共同开拓市场。我们致力于与生态系统中的合作伙伴携手，让机遇集合体变得更加广阔。如今，我们主要服务于报表和商业智能场景，但越来越多公司开始将数据运营化。随着机器学习浪潮的兴起，高质量的Transform数据资产正被用于训练模型，这意味着机遇空间将持续扩大。我们应以此为目标，与各方合作提升市场吸引力，而非将其过度细分。（00:19:37）  
第三个原则是发挥自身优势。我们立志成为平台型公司，深知自己的专长所在，但也为生态系统留出空间，让其他公司为用户提供有价值的解决方案。我们致力于构建一个生态系统，汇聚现代数据栈中的多家公司。总体而言，我们对竞争采取长期观点，仅在两个领域坚守立场：一是Transform标准，二是语义标准。我们相信这两者协同服务能更好地满足用户需求。除此之外，我们相信通过与生态系统合作，我们既能达成自身目标，也能助力合作伙伴实现他们的愿景。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This might be a good time to just chat about dbt and the success the company has had. So many startups have tried to become a standard default layer of what's now called the modern data stack. And I don't know any startup doesn't use dbt or planning to use dbt. It's just a incredibly rare success story somewhere to snowflake where it's just like it's the default for building large data startups and most startups these days work with a lot of data. So my question is just like what do you think dbt did most right to win in this and continue to win?
turns.zh: 现在或许可以聊聊dbt及其取得的成功。许多初创公司都试图成为现代数据栈的标准默认层。我不知道有哪家初创公司不使用dbt或不计划使用dbt。这无疑是一个极其罕见的成功案例，其影响力已渗透至大数据初创企业的基石——如今大多数初创公司都需要处理大量数据。所以我的问题是，dbt做对了哪些关键点才能在竞争中脱颖而出并持续保持领先？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: So I think dbt did a lot of things right, but I'll point out too that really stick out to me. And the first is just power and simplicity and the second is a commitment to being open. And I'll touch on what I mean by those two things. So when dbt was first getting started, you would hear a lot from companies, I don't understand, what's so special about dbt? We have a SQL templating tool at our company, we built one in-house. Like this is really straightforward and simple and it's true like dbt is really simple, but that is the power of it. (00:21:37): So our founders, Tristan, Drew and Connor, they had a belief that the people who do data analysis work, that really work closely with their business stakeholders should also be the ones to contribute to creating clean data assets in production because that data prep work is a necessary prerequisite for any analysis that you do. So dbt was really this belief that if you know SQL, we want to invite you to do these workflows that were traditionally held by data engineers but you had to earn that. So dbt has this nice framework where it's harder to mess up, keeps data quality really high, but it is pretty simple to get started and learn and learn. And that was really the unlock in the industry. We were definitely solving a pain point at the right time. (00:22:26): And then the second thing is this commitment to being open. So dbt is open source and that's the main guts of dbt where you write your business logic and it helps in a number of ways. Specifically it helps with flywheel, keep the flywheel running and also with network effects. And I'll explain what that looks like. So dbt is really easy to get started with at your company with reduced friction. We're building a product that people, so they talk about it, they want to share it both at their organization and with other companies. Other companies get started with dbt again with reduced friction. (00:23:05): We now get to see this really diverse set of use cases for dbt across company sizes, across industries and it allows us to build a truly horizontal company. As our company grows, we get to invest back into our community and our product and the flywheel begins to spin faster. And then meanwhile we have a really large user base. So we have 20,000 companies using dbt every single week and that attracts partners to want to build for dbt and so they share best practices, build workflows, and now if you're a company and you've standardized on dbt, you've really unlocked an integrated modern data ecosystem that wasn't available for you before. So that has a flywheel and also benefits everyone that decides to be on the standard. So it's those two really important trends that made dbt so powerful today.
turns.zh:
因此，我认为 Dbt 在很多方面做得很出色，但我还要指出两点让我印象深刻的地方。首先是其强大的功能性和简洁性，第二是开放共享的理念。接下来，我会分别解释这两点的含义。  

Dbt刚起步时，很多公司都会问："Dbt到底有什么特别之处？我们公司自己开发了SQL模板工具，这不是很简单吗？"确实，Dbt确实简单，但这正是它的强大之处。（00:21:37）  

我们的创始人Tristan、Drew和Connor坚信，真正与业务部门密切合作的数据分析师，应该能够自主创建生产环境中的优质数据资产，因为数据预处理是任何分析工作的必要前提。因此，Dbt秉持这样一个理念：只要你懂SQL，我们就欢迎你来承担传统上由数据工程师负责的工作——但这需要你的努力。Dbt提供了一个易于上手的框架，既能保障数据质量，又能让学习成本极低。这正是行业的突破口。我们在正确的时机解决了行业痛点。  

第二点是开放共享的承诺。Dbt是开源项目，核心部分（编写业务逻辑的部分）能在多个方面带来益处。具体来说，它有助于形成正向循环（flywheel），促进生态效应（network effects）。我来解释一下其原理。Dbt让企业上手成本极低，用户无需大量投入即可快速上手。人们会主动在内部和其他公司分享Dbt经验，形成良性循环。（00:23:05）  

如今，我们见证了Dbt在不同规模的公司、不同行业的广泛应用。这让我们得以构建一个真正横向发展的生态圈。随着公司规模扩大，Dbt不断投入社区和产品研发，良性循环加速。如今每周有2万家公司使用Dbt，这吸引了合作伙伴共同构建生态。标准化Dbt的公司能接入一个前所未有的现代数据生态系统。这形成了一种良性循环，惠及所有采用标准的用户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing there is essentially the product was right for what people needed to solve. There's also a product led component, open source, free self-serve piece that people adopted, used and started working and then scaled and started paying for it. And then there's an alignment of the vision of where this was going and how it fit with how people wanted this to work for them. Is there anything else? Because a lot of startups do that and that all sounds really smart and good, but a lot of startups try to do those things and no one cares. Maybe their product isn't necessarily what people are looking for, maybe they don't get the right distribution. I don't know. Is there anything else that you think they did really well that helped them kickstart this to even be a thing? Is it timing that was really great? Is it specific influencers early on?
turns.zh: 听起来产品正是满足了人们解决问题的需求。产品还具备开源、免费自助服务等特点，用户接受并采用后，逐渐扩大规模并开始付费。同时，产品愿景与用户需求高度契合。还有其他关键因素吗？因为很多初创公司都做过类似尝试，但往往无人问津。或许他们的产品不符合市场需求，或许分发策略失误，我也不确定。你们认为还有哪些成功要素助力了DBT的成功？是时机选择恰到好处吗？还是早期有影响力的人物起到了关键作用？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Yeah. I think timing was really important with the success of dbt. That they were there when the cloud data warehouses were really exploding and growing in an enormous way. And dbt Labs started as Fishtown Analytics, a consulting firm. So they worked really, really closely and hands-on with all of their consulting partners to get the pain point and really solve firsthand challenges that they saw. I think that combination of being at the right place at the right time and also getting to work really closely with people's day-to-day problems created a really special experience.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为时机对DBT的成功至关重要。当时云数据仓库正迎来爆发式增长，而DBT Labs最初是以Fishtown Analytics的身份创立的，这是一家咨询公司。他们与所有咨询合作伙伴密切合作，深入理解客户痛点并亲自解决实际问题。这种在正确时机、紧密接触客户真实需求的组合，创造了独特的成功体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I didn't know that. That's a really important element of the story is basically they were focused... How long did they do that Fishtown Analytics consultancy?
turns.zh: 我之前不知道这点。故事的关键在于他们专注于……Fishtown Analytics咨询业务做了多久？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Board consulting part of the business was almost two years.
turns.zh: 咨询业务部分持续了近两年。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So they basically spent two years solving this problem basically manually for people, and that's such a great way to understand real pain and figure out how to solve it.
turns.zh: 好的，他们花了两年时间手动为客户解决问题，这真是理解真实痛点并找到解决方案的绝佳方式。

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, so that's a really interesting insight. Just spend a few years. It sounds like it was almost manually helping people transform their data using whatever tools already existed.
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以这是一个非常有趣的见解。就花几年时间。听起来他们几乎是手动帮助人们使用现有工具转换数据。

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Yeah. Well, they were building dbt and using dbt to help them do their jobs better and supporting their clients. And whenever they encountered paper cuts or friction or the workflow was taking longer than they expected, they would build that into dbt. And that really matured the experience of the product because the people who were building it, the founders were also day-to-day working with these customers or clients that had pain points.
turns.zh: 是的。他们一边开发DBT，一边用DBT帮助客户提升工作效率。每当遇到效率低下、流程繁琐的问题时，他们就会将其纳入DBT的改进范畴。这种持续迭代的经验积累，让产品体验更加成熟，因为开发者们亲自与客户沟通，理解他们的痛点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That reminds me of a story you told me about how you made your eng team do some manual work of an algorithm involved in transformation. Can you share that?
turns.zh: 这让我想起你之前讲过的故事，你让工程团队手动处理转换算法中的某个问题。能分享一下吗？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Okay. So I'm going to preface this story by sharing that I'm a huge math nerd and one of my favorite books on logic is called Girdle Escher Bach. And in this book there's a fun scene where there's an ant farm that bands together to do the work of a computer flipping bits from zero to one to solve logic gates. So this chapter of that book was really the inspiration for an exercise that I ran my team through. So about a year ago we were doing a big zero to one new project at dbt Labs and we were going to change the algorithm for how we built customers data transformation graphs. And I needed a way for the team to really internalize all of the changes that we were going to be making and I needed them to own it because otherwise they wouldn't be able to anticipate all of the edge cases and it wouldn't be quite as durable. You couldn't copy paste the algorithm. (00:27:41): So I showed up to a team offsite with a spool of rope and sticky notes and I think my team looked at me crazy, went with two heads when I started to tie people up to create a graph. So each note of the graph was an engineer and the rope was the edges of the graph to connect them. And then we worked through the new algorithm extremely slowly, step by step. And it was a way that you couldn't leave that exercise without knowing exactly what was going on because everyone had a role to play. (00:28:16): So I think a lot of times when you're starting something new, you get into a situation where a few people really understand it and they're running way ahead of the rest of the pack. But I needed a way for the whole team to go along for the journey. So I'm constantly trying to create these important moments or memorable moments for the team so that it's centered around our mission and they can have the ownership of taking the project and making it successful. So it was perhaps a overly creative or kooky way to spend the day, but it was really successful.
turns.zh: 好的。首先，我要说我是个数学狂热爱好者，我最喜欢的逻辑学著作之一是《吉德尔·埃舍尔·巴赫》。在书中有一段有趣的场景：一个蚁群通过协作完成了计算机翻转比特的工作，解决逻辑门问题。正是这本书中的这一章节，启发了我为团队设计的一项练习。大约一年前，我们在dbt Labs开展了一个从0到1的重大新项目，计划改变客户数据转换图的构建算法。我需要让团队真正理解即将做出的所有变更，并让他们对此负责，否则他们就无法预料到所有边缘情况，也就难以确保项目的持久性。毕竟算法是不可复制的。（00:27:41）：于是我在团队的异地会议上拿出了一卷绳子和便利贴。我记得当我开始用绳子把人们绑起来搭建图表时，团队成员都惊讶得目瞪口呆。图表中的每个便利贴代表一位工程师，绳子则连接图表的各个节点。我们极其缓慢地逐步研究了新算法。这种方式确保每个人都能清楚理解整个过程，因为每个人都承担着关键角色。（00:28:16）：我认为很多时候，当你开始一个新项目时，总会有少数人理解得很透彻，而其他人则落在后面。但我需要让整个团队共同参与这个过程。因此，我不断为团队创造这些重要时刻或难忘的经历，让项目围绕我们的使命展开，让他们能够主导项目的成功。尽管这或许是一种过于创意或古怪的度过一天的方式，但它确实取得了成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What was the actual algorithm you were trying to implement?
turns.zh: 你们当时到底想实现什么样的算法？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: We were trying to figure out how to make flipping the way that we run people's dags from an imperative way to a declarative way. So instead of running things left to when data arrived in your warehouse. You think about it as reverse, like what would need to happen to make your data SLAs be materialized in time.
turns.zh: 我们试图将处理数据转换图的方式从命令式转换为声明式。也就是说，数据到达仓库后，我们不再被动响应，而是反向思考：要实现数据SLA，必须采取哪些措施？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And sounds like the team found that valuable.
turns.zh: 太棒了。听起来团队觉得这很有价值。

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Reminds me of a clip from this last season of Ted Lasso where they have used red strings and I won't get into it, but if you've seen it you will know what I'm talking about. I want to come back to your chatting about open source versus not open source. So some part of dbt was is open source and some isn't. I'm curious how the team decides what is open source and what should be open source, what isn't open source and what to charge for?
turns.zh: 好的。这让我想起了《特德·拉索》上一季的一个片段，他们用了红绳子来传递信息。我就不详细说了，如果你看过那部剧，就会明白我在说什么。我想回到你之前提到的开源与非开源的讨论。dbt的一些部分是开源的，而有些则不是。我很好奇团队是如何决定哪些部分是开源，哪些不该开源，哪些部分收费的？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: We think about dbt open source. It's really the guts of the data transformation. It's where you describe your business logic. And then on the cloud side we build proprietary software that supercharges the development life cycle and the productionization of dbt at scale. So what we think about as leaving for our cloud offering is we deal with state, so stateful interactions and also any cross team or structural collaboration. We want to reserve that for our proprietary offering. And I think it's really important to have that distinction of what do you believe should be open source or what is the open standard that really matters? And ecosystem to us is really important. So it's important that that remains open source, but then we want to supercharge that experience with an open core model and build proprietary software that makes people much more successful at using dbt.
turns.zh: 我们思考了数据库转换工具（dbt）的开源问题。dbt实际上是数据转换的核心部分，您可以在其中描述自己的业务逻辑。然后在云端，我们开发专有软件，极大地加速了dbt的开发周期和大规模生产化进程。因此，我们认为云端产品应专注于处理状态问题——即有状态交互以及跨团队或结构性协作。我们希望将这些功能保留给专有产品。对我而言，区分哪些功能应开源、哪些才是真正重要的开放标准至关重要。生态系统对我们来说同样重要。因此，保持dbt开源非常重要，但我们希望通过开放核心模型来提升用户体验，并开发专有软件，助力用户更高效地使用dbt。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today's episode is brought to you by AssemblyAI. If you're looking to build AI powered features in your audio and video products, then you need to know about AssemblyAI, which makes it easy to transcribe and understand speech at scale. What I love about AssemblyAI is you can use their simple API to access the latest AI breakthroughs from top tier research labs. Product team that startups and enterprises are using AssemblyAI to automatically transcribe and summarize phone calls and virtual meetings, detect topics in podcasts, pinpoint when sensitive content spoken and lots more. All of AssemblyAI's models which are accessed through their API are production ready. (00:31:26): So many PMs I know are considering or already building with AI and AssemblyAI is the fastest way to build with AI for audio use cases. Now's the time to check out AssemblyAI, which makes it easy to bring the highest accuracy transcription plus valuable insights to your customers. Just like Spotify, CallRail and writer do for theirs. Visit assemblyai.com/lenny to try their API for free and start testing their models with their no code playground. That's assemblyai.com/lenny. I know you also spent a lot of time thinking about pricing and willingness to pay and things along those lines. (00:32:03): Is there anything you could share about which is what you've learned about how to think about pricing for a tool like this or even in general?
turns.zh: 今天的节目由AssemblyAI赞助。如果您希望在音频和视频产品中构建AI驱动的功能，那么您需要了解AssemblyAI。AssemblyAI能让您轻松大规模地转录和理解语音内容。我最欣赏AssemblyAI的地方在于，您可以通过其简单易用的API，获取顶级研究实验室的最新AI突破成果。许多初创公司和企业的产品团队都在使用AssemblyAI自动转录和摘要电话会议及虚拟会议内容，检测播客中的主题，精确识别敏感内容等等情况。通过API访问的所有AssemblyAI模型都已做好生产准备。（00:31:26）：我认识的许多产品经理都在考虑或已经在使用AI进行开发，而AssemblyAI是音频用例中最快的AI开发途径。现在正是尝试AssemblyAI的绝佳时机，它能轻松为您的客户带来最高准确度的转录和宝贵的洞察。正如Spotify、CallRail和writer为他们的客户所做的那样。访问assemblyai.com/lenny即可免费试用他们的API，并在无代码平台上测试他们的模型。网址是assemblyai.com/lenny。我知道您也花了大量时间思考定价和用户支付意愿等相关问题。（00:32:03）：您能否分享一下您在为这类工具定价时所学到的经验，或者更广泛地谈谈您的见解？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Pricing and willingness to pay is such a hard conversation and lots of startups don't do this early enough in their company journey. Likely a side effect of zero interest rates where investors were happy funding GitHub stars and usage and companies never thought about how am I going to make revenue or make money, which is it's important. So for us at dbt Labs, I don't claim to be perfect at it, but we're trying to get a better muscle around it. And I always think about Madhavan who wrote this book Pricing Innovation. I know you've had him on the show before, but he shares that you don't get to decide if you're going to have a pricing or willingness to pay a conversation. You only get to decide what. So it's much better to have that conversation before you build the product than have it when your sales team's trying to sell something and people aren't excited about what you've built, aren't willing to pay for it. (00:33:04): And at dbt Labs we have this value, it's one of our core values that says we are more concerned with value creation than value capture. And we really mean this. When we talk about what is the value of dbt Labs to our customers, they often talk about how it's either 20 to 35% as valuable as what they spend on their cloud data warehouse. But what we charge our customers is a very small fraction of that 20 to 35% and that's by design. And last year we did our first ever pricing change in the company history and you learn a tremendous amount when you have that event because you get to test the price elasticity by of your customers. (00:33:49): And it's so important to learn that lesson while the company is still smaller or the stakes are lower because pricing just is always evolving. It's not a fixed thing, it gets more complex over time. So we have to think about it quite a bit because my team builds proprietary software for dbt cloud and when we lose a deal we most often lose it to dbt open source and we like it that way. We're happy to lose to ourselves, but we have to really think very deeply about what are people willing to pay for and what moves the needle for them and focus on that.
turns.zh:
定价和客户支付意愿的讨论实在不易，许多初创公司在公司发展初期就未能重视这方面问题。很可能这是零利率政策的副作用——当时投资者乐于为GitHub上的“星标”和用户量提供资金，企业从未思考过如何盈利或创造收入，而这恰恰至关重要。因此，在dbt Labs，我们不自诩在这方面做得完美，但我们正努力提升这方面的能力。我总是想起马达万（Madhavan）写的《定价创新》一书。我知道你之前邀请过他上节目，但他提到，你无法决定是否要进行定价或客户支付意愿的讨论，但你只能决定讨论的内容。因此，在产品开发前就开展这项对话，要比等销售团队试图推销产品却发现客户对产品不感兴趣、更不愿为之付费的情况好得多。

（00:33:04）在dbt Labs，我们秉持这样一项核心价值观：我们更关注价值创造而非价值捕获。我们是认真的。当客户谈及dbt Labs的价值时，他们常说其价值相当于客户在云数据仓库上花费的20%至35%。但我们向客户收取的费用只是这一价值的极小部分，这是有意为之。去年，我们在公司历史上首次调整定价策略，当你经历这样的事件时，能深刻体会到客户对价格弹性的反应。这一点至关重要，因为在公司规模较小、风险较低时，学习成本更低。定价始终在不断演变，并非一成不变，随着时间推移会变得更加复杂。因此，我们必须深入思考这些问题。我的团队为dbt云平台开发专有软件，当我们失去某笔交易时，往往输给dbt开源版本。我们乐于输给自己，但必须深入思考客户愿意为哪些功能买单，以及哪些功能能真正推动业务发展，并以此为核心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm so curious what that pricing process was like to figure out what to change. Is there anything you could share about just what that was for you or what are some just surprises that came out of that process or just like, "Wow, we didn't expect that in these conversations?"
turns.zh: 我很好奇你们是如何确定需要调整定价策略的。有没有什么具体经验可以分享？比如，在这个过程中有没有意外发现，或者有没有那种“哇，我们没想到在这些对话中会遇到这种情况”的时刻？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: It's really like an all hands on deck conversation. Pricing is so cross-cutting because it's a finance discussion as well. You're modeling out things in spreadsheets and figuring out how that might impact the business. But you can't just solve these problems in spreadsheets. You have to go talk to customers, test the waters, understand where people's appetites are and sussing that out is really hard. And then of course there's a product piece to it too where you have to affect it and communicate it as well. So it was very cross-cutting. We learned a lot. We track our conversion rates really carefully. We track our turn rates very carefully and I think largely we were happy with the change that we made and we felt like one of the big things that we were trying to solve for was have our pricing catch up to how people valued the tool.
turns.zh: 这确实是一场全员参与的讨论。定价涉及多个领域，因为这也是财务层面的讨论。你需要在电子表格中模拟各种情景，评估其对业务的影响。但仅靠电子表格无法解决这些问题。你必须与客户沟通，试探他们的意愿，了解他们的真实需求，而这实在不易。当然，产品层面也需要同步调整，既要实施新方案，又要做好沟通。因此，整个过程需要多部门协作。我们学到了很多。我们非常仔细地追踪转化率和流失率。总体而言，我们对所做的调整感到满意。我们试图解决的核心问题之一，就是让我们的定价体系与客户对产品的价值认知相匹配。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How many people did you end up talking to, who was doing these conversations and is there anything really important you learned about how to ask these questions and these sorts of leanness to pay conversations?
turns.zh: 你们最终和多少人进行了交谈？都是哪些人在参与这些对话？在如何提问以及这些轻松随意的谈话中，你们有没有收获什么重要见解？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: So we talked to dozens. It was combination of product and product marketing, having the conversations and people aren't very willing to share explicitly what they will pay. But there's some tools that we use on relative value. People most think about what is the relative value of dbt in their cloud warehouse. And we also tried to employ some of the tactics that we tried to suss out what do people view as very inexpensive? What's a price point that's very cheap or a no-brainer? What price point is maybe fair or comfortable for them and what would be too expensive? And then we had all the data back to figure out where we landed.
turns.zh: 所以我们和几十个人进行了交流。这些对话涉及产品和产品营销，人们通常不太愿意明确分享他们愿意支付的价格。但我们确实运用了相对价值评估的工具。大多数人都在思考，dbt在他们的云仓库中的相对价值是多少。我们还尝试了一些策略，试图搞清楚人们认为什么价格非常便宜？什么价格点是极低且无需犹豫的？什么价格对他们来说可能公平或舒适，而什么价格又太高了？然后我们汇总所有数据，得出最终结论。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to M&A for a bit. I had a few more questions there and I moved on from that. So again, you've done a lot of work within the M&A realm. Something that I saw recently, and this connects to the fact that a lot of startups now are looking to get sold. This VC hunter walk, he's a founder of Home Brew Ventures, had this interesting blog post where he basically suggested you should actually think about being public about the fact that you're selling your company. Which is crazy because in the past you never want to come across as too selly. I don't want people to think I'm desperate. And his point is many startups are desperate right now and it's okay to be public about that. And then in theory creates more of a bidding situation where many people know versus keeping it secret and in closed rooms. So my question is just what do you think of that? Do you think that's effective strategy? Is it not?
turns.zh: 我想再回过头来谈谈并购领域。我之前对此有几个问题，然后就转到其他话题了。所以再次说，你们在并购领域做了很多工作。最近我注意到一件事，这与现在许多初创公司急于出售自身业务的事实有关。VC猎手沃克（Home Brew Ventures的创始人）在一篇有趣的博文中建议，实际上你应该公开表明自己正在出售公司。这听起来很疯狂，因为过去人们总是不想显得太急切，生怕别人认为自己走投无路。但他的观点是，现在许多初创公司确实走投无路，所以公开这一事实是可以的。相比之下，如果保密的话，反而会让更多人蒙在鼓里。所以我的问题是，你们对此怎么看？你们认为这是一个有效的策略吗？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: I think it's good advice. If you're in a Hail Mary situation where you're looking for a home or you need an exit for your business, it's better to be transparent and cast a wider net. And you're right, in previous times founders tried to be a little bit cute or obfuscate that they were evasive the situation that they were in because they wanted to drum up some competitive interest when there really wasn't any. But unfortunately in today's climate, too many companies are in that spot so it's impossible to hide it. So the better approach is just to be transparent and I see it pretty regularly and there's absolutely no shame in sending a note that says something like, "Hey, we're looking for an exit for our company X, Y, and Z didn't pan out as we expected. We built a really interesting product and we want to keep the team together. We're running a process. Are you interested?" Really just as simple as that.
turns.zh: 我认为这是个好建议。如果你处在孤注一掷的境地，正在寻找退出机会，或者需要为公司寻找出路，那么保持透明并扩大搜索范围是更好的选择。你说得对，过去有些创始人试图耍点小聪明，含糊其辞，掩饰自己所处的困境，因为他们想激发一些竞争兴趣，但实际上根本没有竞争。然而不幸的是，在当今环境下，太多公司都处在这种境地，所以隐藏事实是不可能的。所以更好的方法就是保持透明。我经常看到这样的情况，没有什么可羞耻的，比如发送一封邮件，内容类似：“嘿，我们正在为公司寻找退出机会，X、Y、Z的尝试没有达到预期。我们开发了一个非常有趣的产品，希望团队能继续在一起。我们正在推进这个过程，你有兴趣吗？” 就这么简单。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've seen a lot of companies put together these really detailed decks or even websites of just like, here's the team, here's what we built to be very promotional about it. Is that something you've seen? Is that something you'd recommend?
turns.zh: 我见过很多公司制作了非常详细的演示文稿，甚至是网站，展示团队和产品，宣传效果很好。你们见过这种情况吗？推荐这样做吗？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Yeah. Usually in these situations people are acquiring the teams and so having your data room together, really the most important thing is these are the team members that are going to come along with the acquisition is the biggest motivator for why a buyer would get excited.
turns.zh: 是的。通常在这种情况下，人们收购的是团队。因此，整理好数据室，展示团队成员将随收购一同加入，这是吸引买家的最大动力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You made this point earlier that a lot of the seeds need to be planted early for you to have the best outcome. And this reminded me... So I had a startup local mine that we sold to Airbnb and I met Airbnb initially at a year before we actually started exploring the process at a random party at South by Southwest where I was, I actually have no memory of this party, but the head of product at Airbnb, Joe bought, remembered it and came back to us a year later and just like, "Hey, what are you guys up to? Maybe we could collaborate on some stuff," and that led to an acquisition. So I think that's just wanted to touch a ban on that point of just the power of, the way I thought about it is let a thousand flowers bloom, just like meet everyone. Get the word out that you're around and what you're doing so that in the future when someone has that problem they're like, "That company, maybe we should talk to them."
turns.zh: 你之前提到过，很多种子需要早期播种才能获得最佳结果。这让我想起……我曾创办过一家本地矿业初创公司，后来将其出售给Airbnb。最初，我是在西南偏南音乐节（SXSW）的一次随意聚会上结识Airbnb的产品负责人乔·博伊尔（Joe Boyle）的。我对那次聚会毫无印象，但乔却记住了我们，并在一年后主动联系我们，问道：“你们在做什么？或许我们可以合作。”最终促成了收购。我想借此机会强调一点：要放眼全局，多多社交，让人们了解你的存在，这样当他们遇到问题时，就会想起你。

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Yeah, you want to make sure that the buyer knows who you are before the acquisition moment and hopefully that's because you've made an impact and they like what you're building. Maybe you've inflicted some pain on them. But yeah, certainly creating those connections well ahead of an exit event is important.
turns.zh: 是的，你要确保潜在买家在收购前就认识你。这通常是因为你已经产生了影响，他们认可你的产品，或许甚至曾被你的创新理念刺痛过。但提前建立这些联系对退出时至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And specifically there it's meet people at your competitors potentially. For us, Airbnb was never even a potential company we would sell to because it had nothing to do with it but ended up making sense down the road. What's like the realm of the companies and people that you think people should think about meeting?
turns.zh: 具体来说，可能需要主动接触竞争对手。对我来说，Airbnb最初并非潜在收购目标，但后来合作的契机出现了。你认为还有哪些公司或人值得接触？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: If the company is buying a lot or they're active, they often have corp dev teams and so use that corp dev team to your advantage. It's their job to meet absolutely every company that could be potentially interested. So take that meeting, say you're not interested in an acquisition just yet, but push them to make an introduction to someone that could sponsor the deal. So usually that's someone in product or maybe a GM and use that as a starting point for maybe just a conversation, maybe something more like a partnership but get the corp dev team to work for you.
turns.zh: 如果公司规模较大或活跃，他们通常有企业发展团队。利用这些团队的资源很重要——他们的职责是主动接触所有可能感兴趣的公司。即使你暂时对收购不感兴趣，也要推动他们为你引荐潜在合作方。例如，产品团队或总经理，这些都是合作的切入点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What if you're at the other end of the spectrum and you're in dire straits right now and you're just like, "Man, what do we do to potentially sell this company?" I know odds are not going to be great, but just what do you suggest folks do in terms of I guess finding connections to potential companies that might be acquirers?
turns.zh: 如果公司正处于困境，急于出售怎么办？我知道成功概率不高，但对于寻求潜在收购方的联系，你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Yeah. I mean use your network. Usually your venture capitalist has a really big network and one of the things that I hear founders feeling the most nervous about is a duty to return the money to the investors. And maybe this is a unpopular thing to say on a podcast, but your investors understand that they're not making their money back. And what they want to do instead is have you end up at a really great company like an Airbnb because that will help them down the road. So it's all about the long game, but use your investors to help you find connections at different companies that could be buying and don't worry so much about disappointing them or being really realistic about where you are in your company journey.
turns.zh: 是的，利用人脉网络。通常你的风投机构人脉广泛。创始人最担心的往往是退出时如何回报投资款。可能这在播客上不太受欢迎，但投资方理解他们无法收回全部资金。他们更希望看到你加入像Airbnb这样的优秀公司，这对他们未来更有利。所以要着眼长远，利用投资方帮助你接触潜在买家，同时不要太在意是否会让他们失望，要实事求是地看待公司发展阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To build on that, I'm just an angel investor, I'm not like the lead fund and they feel differently I imagine. But the last thing I want for a founders to get stuck at a company they hate and just so that they could return some money or have some outcome rather they just give up, move on. Life is short.
turns.zh: 基于此，我只是一个天使投资人，我和那些领投基金的情况不同，我想他们可能有不同的看法。但我最不希望看到创始人被困在自己不喜欢的公司里，只是为了回本或取得某种结果而苦苦挣扎，最终选择放弃，另谋出路。人生短暂。

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Yeah. I think founders forget that it is so risky investing in early stage companies that 50% of portfolios investments don't return anything. And that's just part of the game and it's a very acceptable path where hey, we gave it our best shot. It didn't work out and moving on.
turns.zh: 是啊。我认为创始人往往忘记，投资早期公司风险极高——50%的投资组合根本无法获得回报。这不过是商业游戏的一部分，也是可以接受的路径：我们尽了全力，但最终未能成功，那就继续前行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which is tough a lot of times for founders that are told like it's all about grit and not giving up and don't quit. Sometimes you should quit.
turns.zh: 这对创始人来说往往很艰难，他们被告知必须要有坚韧不拔的精神，永不放弃，永不退缩。但有时确实应该选择退出。

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Gosh, yeah. I don't want to say that. I think being founders, it's an extremely lonely role sometimes and it is very hard to know what your next chapter will look like or what the journey will look like and sometimes you really are out of cash and you do have to find a home. But I hope that you can continue to fight and find a way forward.
turns.zh: 天啊，是啊。我不想这么说。但我认为作为创始人，有时这是一个极其孤独的角色，很难预见下一步的路会怎样，或者旅程会如何发展。有时你真的资金告急，必须寻找出路。但我希望你们能继续奋斗，找到前进的方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Agreed. Specifically for people thinking about selling their company, are there any companies you think are good companies for people to look at right now that are actively acquiring or open to M&A?
turns.zh: 同意。特别是对于那些考虑出售公司的人来说，有没有什么好公司值得关注？目前有哪些公司正在积极收购或对并购持开放态度？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: This is a tough one. I think a lot of companies are on the sidelines for a number of reasons. And they could be on the sidelines because they just did an acquisition and they're trying to digest or integrate that company. They could be on the sidelines because they're not growing headcount as much and M&A is often org chart gymnastics of folding the target companies headcount into your budget and plan and maybe just don't have a lot of space. Or probably more common right now is there's just a general uncertainty about the future. And in highly volatile markets people want to take care of their own and even the best M&A deals at a level of complexity that a lot of buyers are just not looking to take on right now. (00:44:07): So there are a number of reasons why people might sit out, but what I would do if I were in a position of wanting to sell my company is I would come up with a buyer set of maybe a dozen and really there aren't more than a dozen companies that will find what you're doing to be a very good fit. Start with your buyer set and then start calling the list by looking at some of the criteria that might count people out. And then go have those conversations. And if you're in a Hail Mary situation, be very transparent about it. Maybe open up the buyer list. But if you still have some room, I would maybe focus on two to three partner or buyers and really play a different playbook, which is inflict pain. Make it really hard for them to not notice you but do it with a smile and be friendly at while you do that.
turns.zh: 这确实是个难题。我认为很多公司出于多种原因暂停行动。可能是因为刚完成收购，正在消化或整合目标公司；也可能是因为扩张放缓，而并购通常意味着将目标公司的员工规模整合到自己的预算和规划中，这或许会让空间变得有限。或者更常见的是，对未来存在普遍的不确定性。在高度波动的市场中，人们倾向于自保，即便是最复杂的并购交易，许多买家目前也无意承接。（00:44:07）：因此，有多种原因导致公司暂停行动。但如果我想出售公司，我会先列出约十家潜在买家——真正适合你的公司不超过十家。从这份买家名单入手，根据一些筛选标准逐步排除，再与这些公司展开对话。如果你处在绝望的境地，要坦诚相告。或许可以开放买家名单。但如果还有回旋余地，我会专注于两到三家合作伙伴或买家，采取不同的策略——制造压力。让他们不得不注意到你，但要保持微笑和友好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sometimes with M&A discussions, there's a lot of subtlety to the way you communicate where you don't come out and be like, please we'd love to sell our company to you. Any advice on just the phrasing and how to approach it or do you think it's just, it's fine, just tell us we're looking to sell our company. Are you interested in being buyer?
turns.zh: 有时候在并购讨论中，沟通方式需要微妙，不能直言“我们想把公司卖给你们”。对于措辞和沟通方式有什么建议吗？还是认为只要诚实地说出“我们想出售公司”就行？你们有兴趣成为买家吗？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Yeah. I just wouldn't be too clever here. Everyone understands like I'm evaluating strategic alternatives. It means you're looking to sell your company and it depends. Do you have time? If you have time, yeah. Don't come out and say, "Hey, I'm for sale." That's not going to end up in a good outcome. But depends where you are in your company journey. If you have time, then don't talk about M&A at all. That's the last thing that you want to speak about. Instead, you're talking about maybe collaborating or partnerships. How do we work together? Knowledge sharing and M&A is a dirty word if you have a lot of runway and you're going to try to continue to pursue an independent path, but if you're out of time, you're out of time.
turns.zh: 是啊。在这种情况下还是别太聪明了。大家都明白我在评估战略选择。这意味着你打算出售公司，但具体情况要看实际情况。你们有时间吗？如果有时间，那没问题。但别直接说"我公司待售"，这样结果不会太好。得看你公司发展到哪一步了。如果有时间，那就别提并购的事。这是最不该谈的话题。相反，你可以考虑合作或建立伙伴关系。比如怎么合作？知识共享之类的。但如果你们还有充足发展空间，坚持独立发展路线，那并购就是个贬义词。不过如果没时间了，那就只能另辟蹊径了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such good advice. I remember the term we used was we want to explore a strategic partnership and everyone's just like, I knows what you mean by that, but you just don't want to say it.
turns.zh: 这建议真棒。我记得我们当时用的术语是"探索战略合作伙伴关系"，大家都懂你的意思，但就是不愿明说。

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Yeah. It's like everyone in the room's looking like yeah. Okay. Strategic partnership or a strategic alternative, it's like we all know these code words and we understand the situation you're in.
turns.zh: 是啊。在场每个人都心领神会。战略合作伙伴关系或战略替代方案，这些暗语大家都懂，彼此心照不宣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. When do you think M&A market might pick up again? I know it's impossible to predict. Do you have any sense?
turns.zh: 是啊。你觉得并购市场何时会回暖？我知道这没法预测，但你有没有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: Yeah. I wish I had a magic ball. That'd be pretty sweet. I think what is happening though is we're far enough out from the peak of the markets. So the peak was really November of 2021. And why does that matter? Two things. One, founders are coming to terms with valuations that they maybe received at the highest of the market, are no longer going to hold in this market and companies are out of cash or maybe out of options. We'll be better assets entering the market soon. And at a certain point the opportunities will just be too great. That will incentivize a lot of the buyers that have been on the bench to start participating again in the M&A market. And I don't know exactly when that will be, but I think we're pretty close. I think we're pretty close.
turns.zh: 是啊。我也希望能有个魔法水晶球。那样就太棒了。不过现在市场离高点已经很远了。市场高点是2021年11月。为什么这很重要？两个原因。一是创始人们不得不面对市场高点时的估值，这些估值在当前市场环境下已不再适用，公司要么现金告急，要么选项用完。很快就会有更优质的资产进入市场。到某个时候，机会就会变得极为丰厚。这会促使许多观望中的买家重返并购市场。不过具体何时还不好说，但我觉得已经很近了。非常近了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you mentioned a value that you have at dbt. I forget exactly what it was, but I'm curious what are the other values that you have at dbt, whatever you can share. Always curious what principles and values companies come down to help drive the way they think.
turns.zh: 你提到了dbt的价值观。我忘了具体内容，但我很好奇dbt还有哪些价值观，如果方便的话可以分享一下。总是好奇公司秉持哪些原则和价值观来指导决策。

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: The value that I shared is we are more concerned with value creation than value capture and that really drives everything that we do. We try to put a lot of good out into the world and it pays back slowly. The whole mission of dbt Labs is to help analytics engineers disseminate organizational knowledge through data. So we really believe also being participants of sharing that information and getting more people knowledgeable about all sorts of things. (00:48:13): Transparency wins. We're a really transparent company. We share our board decks. We have lots of communication and participation in all of our Slacks. We're writing culture. We have hard conversations in the open. So that's another a big one. Transparency always wins. We are humble. We don't ever feel like we are successful. We come at this from a very humble space where we feel like we have to serve our community and our users and that really motivates us. And then another one is just work done well as its own end and it's really focusing on the journey and not the end destination.
turns.zh: 我所分享的价值观是，我们更关注价值创造而非价值获取，这真正驱动着我们所做的一切。我们努力为世界贡献价值，而这种价值会逐渐回馈给我们。dbt Labs的使命是帮助分析工程师通过数据传播组织知识。因此，我们坚信参与信息共享、让更多人掌握各类知识也非常重要。（00:48:13）：透明度至上。我们是一家非常透明的公司。我们会分享董事会演示文稿，在Slack中保持高频沟通与参与。我们致力于打造企业文化，公开进行艰难对话。这也是一项核心原则——透明度永远胜出。我们保持谦逊，从不自视成功。我们怀着服务社区和用户的初心，才得以持续前行。此外，高质量的工作本身就是目标，我们更关注过程而非终点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I want to do a post someday of just like, here's the values all these different successful companies have come to and see if there's any patterns. I'm actually doing a post right now on Snowflake and on Figma and what you touched on. There's such a connection and a thread of obsessing with your users and making sure they're happy at Figma. I forget exactly what it is, but it's just like in this article, it's going to come out tomorrow actually. So people get a sense of when we recorded this where they think of their company as software as a service where service is their number one goal. They actually provide service and software is just a way to do that. And then it's Snowflake. Their number one core value is put customers first and they talk a lot about how they just actually informs their prioritization all I think, and all their thinking. So it's interesting. That also comes up a lot in what you're talking about, which I think it's easy to say, but I think what actually separates companies that succeed is they actually put this into practice.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我希望未来能写一篇帖子，汇总这些成功企业的价值观，观察其共性。比如，我现在正在写一篇关于Snowflake和Figma的帖子，内容与你提到的理念高度契合。Figma在关注用户体验、确保用户满意度方面做得极其出色，这让我印象深刻。虽然具体细节我记不太清，但正如这篇明天即将发布的文章所指出的，Snowflake将客户放在首位，这一核心价值观深刻影响着他们的优先事项和决策。再看dbt Labs，他们的核心价值观是“以客户为先”，深刻体现在产品设计与服务理念中。有趣的是，你提到的这些理念与成功企业的共性有很多相通之处，虽然道理听起来简单，但真正能让企业成功的关键在于将这些理念落到实处。

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: It's really interesting too because a lot of the people who work at dbt Labs came from the community, so they feel this real ownership in making the experience an excellent one because they were so compelled to come join dbt Labs because the product changed the way that they work or changed their lives. So that commitment to the community and product experience is really, really strong.
turns.zh: dbt Labs的许多员工都是从社区中成长起来的，因此他们对打造卓越的用户体验有着强烈的责任感，因为正是产品的变革改变了他们的工作方式，甚至改变了他们的生活。这种对社区和产品体验的承诺确实非常坚定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This isn't another thread. Maybe we'll go down real quick. I'm working on a different post around Reddit and how to work with really opinionated users that strong opinions about changes to the product and the way they described it, these guys were there for five years working with the community on the product. Is that to your users, the product is their baby, basically. It's like they think it's theirs versus the companies. And I'm curious, having a really strong opinionated community, what it sounds like you also have, what have you learned about just working with them to build product that makes them happy and avoid revolts and really upsetness?
turns.zh: 这不是另一个话题分支。或许我们可以快速回归正题。我正在写一篇关于Reddit的帖子，探讨如何与那些对产品变更和设计有强烈意见的用户打交道。这些用户在产品上与社区合作了五年。对你们来说，产品就是他们的孩子，用户与公司之间存在着本质上的区别。我很好奇，面对这样有强烈意见的社区，你们是如何与他们合作，打造让他们满意的产品，避免引发反抗和不满情绪的？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: It's hard as you grow. I think it's just a challenge cause our community gets bigger. You can't service everybody's needs. But I think what we've done is everyone is very deep in our own product. I think one of the cool stats is at dbt Labs we have over 30% of our employee headcount has contributed to our data transformation workflow. So that's across every discipline. It's in obviously product, obviously in our data team. Our marketing team also contributes to data transformation. And our engineering team will also contribute to our internal dbt analytics project and that sense of really understanding what the experience is like and then soliciting as much feedback as we possibly can. We have a dbt Slack community of 50,000 and all of our employees are in that Slack channel regularly and can feel when we mess up or we don't quite deliver an experience that we're proud of, you will just see dozens of people trying to jump on board and try to make it better.
turns.zh: 成长的过程中确实会遇到挑战。我觉得这只不过是成长的必经之路，因为我们的社区规模不断扩大。你不可能满足所有人的需求。但我认为我们做得很成功——每个团队成员都深度参与了我们的产品开发。一个很酷的数据是，在dbt Labs，超过30%的员工都为我们的数据转换工作流做出了贡献。这涵盖了各个领域——产品团队、数据团队、营销团队，甚至工程团队也会参与我们的内部dbt分析项目。我们会尽可能深入了解用户体验，并收集尽可能多的反馈。我们有5万人的dbt Slack社区，所有员工都会定期参与其中，当我们出现失误或未能提供令人满意的体验时，总会有数十人主动参与改进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there any other frameworks or just general processes that you found to be release useful in building awesome product running teams?
turns.zh: 在组建优秀的产品团队时，还有其他框架或通用流程能发挥作用吗？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: I'm not a big framework person, but there's two sayings that I find myself repeating or I either to myself or to others. And it's worse is better and tech debt is a champagne problem. And what do I mean by that? It's really to help me combat this perfectionism because perfect doesn't exist and you should instead go with good enough because when you ship, that's the moment when you get to learn a lot from your users and you just can't anticipate it. You try very hard to understand exactly how people will use the product and get all the edges ironed out. But you can't until you ship. And I'll share an example. So my team helps support the dbt cloud scheduler and the initial version of the dbt cloud scheduler was pretty naive. We were a little embarrassed by it. (00:53:02): It was a big old for loop over a big old jobs table. So we would look like is it time for this job to run? Okay. Yes, run this job. Okay. It's not time for this job to run next, continue on. Is it time? Yes, run this job. And it would just loop over and it's extremely naive and very simple, but it got the job done. And I try to remind the engineers, we would be so lucky to have tech debt because that means people are using the product. And now we've had to rebuild our scheduler several times over because we do have meaningful scale. We have 8,000 companies using our scheduler. We have to manage 10 million runs per month. But what we didn't need at launch was a distributed scheduler with coworkers and RabbitMQ. We just didn't need it because we had no users. So these two sayings that worse is better and tech debt is a champagne problem, just really reminds people like, let's ship, let's get it out into the user's hands and then we'll learn and iterate and it'll be a better experience for them.
turns.zh: 我不太热衷于框架，但有两句话我常挂在嘴边——“越糟糕越好”和“技术债务是香槟问题”。这两句话的含义是什么？它们帮助我克服完美主义，因为完美是不存在的，你应该追求“足够好”。因为当产品上线时，你才能从用户那里获得大量反馈，而这些反馈是无法预料的。你可能绞尽脑汁去理解用户如何使用产品，消除所有边缘问题，但直到产品上线才能做到。我举个例子。我的团队负责支持dbt云调度器，最初版本非常简陋，我们对此感到有些尴尬。（00:53:02）：它就是一个大循环，不断遍历一个大任务表。例如，检查这个任务是否该运行了？是的，运行这个任务。然后继续检查下一个任务是否该运行了？是的，运行这个任务。如此循环往复。虽然非常简单粗暴，但确实能完成任务。我提醒工程师们，拥有技术债务是幸运的，因为这意味着产品有人在用。而现在我们不得不多次重建调度器，因为我们已经有了规模。8000家公司在使用我们的调度器，每月要处理1000万次运行任务。但上线时我们不需要分布式调度器、消息队列和RabbitMQ，因为当时根本没有用户。所以“越糟糕越好”和“技术债务是香槟问题”这两句话，真正提醒人们：先上线，再交到用户手中，然后不断学习迭代，这样才能为用户带来更好的体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a good segue to my last question. So weren't a PM before this role. You have strong experience in investing, investment banking business in general. I'm curious what you think product managers should maybe focus on more or learn more or lean into to become stronger product leaders based on the experience you've had moving into product.
turns.zh: 这正好引出我的最后一个问题。你之前不是产品经理，但在投资领域有丰富的经验。我很好奇，基于你转入产品经理的经验，你认为产品经理应该更关注什么、学习什么或深耕哪些领域，才能成为更强大的产品领导者？

turns.speaker: Julia Schottenstein
turns.en: So I pull a lot on my experience or some of the things that I did was as an investor in my current role in product. And maybe I'll touch on what is the scale of a venture capitalist might be a little bit foreign for people, but venture capitalists, they spend all their day meeting lots of different companies, context switching. They have to know a little bit about quite a lot of different things. And they do this to refine their investment tastes or find their investor judgment. And they're also investing a lot in their network and connecting people, supporting people, and mining people for ideas that are way smarter than they are. So you do that all the time in Venture and I've brought a lot of those skills with me into product and it translates really well. (00:55:17): The first is I still spend a lot of time investing in my network and I think it's an underrated way for a PM to spend their time. And I try to build a network of operators at other companies that are like dbt Labs that are growing nicely, maybe a little bit ahead of where we are. And I ask them questions, how did you navigate open source? How did you navigate pricing? How did you navigate acquisitions? And then I take the best ideas, figure out which ones I can apply and bring it back to dbt Labs. The second thing is I really think my special T or my superpower is that I'm a T-shaped generalist. So I know a little about a lot of things from finance to business to product. I have to go a lot deeper in product in the areas that I specialize in. That's where the tail of the tea comes in. But it's precisely because I've had a diverse background that makes me more effective when I'm trying to get things done within the organization. Because I have just more credible experiences that I can pull from. (00:56:18): And then the last thing that I think maybe doesn't show up day to day in my product work, but in investing, you're constantly thinking about risk and the power laws, and we touched on this before, but most investments don't work out. You lose the dollars that you put in, but all the returns come from these rare events that make up for all the losses. You have to think about what are the uncapped upside opportunities in investing. And I think in product, you still have to do the same thing. If 50% of the things I worked on went to zero, we'd have a problem. But it encourages me to continue to make bets for the company that has the chance of bending the trajectory of our business.
turns.zh: 接下来，我会谈谈自己的经验，或者说我在当前产品角色中作为投资者所做的一些事情。或许我会讲讲风险投资家的规模对人们来说可能有些陌生，但风险投资家每天都要与众多公司会面，频繁切换工作场景。他们必须对众多领域略知一二，以此来磨练投资眼光、提升判断力。同时，他们还需大量投入人脉资源，帮助他人、支持他人，挖掘比自己更具智慧的创意。这些技能在风险投资领域日复一日地被磨砺，而我将其中许多技能带入了产品领域，并且效果显著。（00:55:17）首先，我仍会投入大量时间拓展人脉网，我认为这是产品经理高效利用时间的低调之道。比如，我会主动与其他快速发展的公司（如dbt Labs）中的运营者建立联系，询问他们如何驾驭开源项目、定价策略、收购策略等问题。然后，从中汲取最佳实践，应用于dbt Labs。第二点，我认为自己的特长在于T型人才——既通晓金融、商业、产品等多领域，又能在专业领域深耕。这正是“茶尾效应”的体现。正因如此，多元背景使我在组织内执行任务时更具效率，因为我能调用更多可靠的经验。（00:56:18）最后，虽然产品工作中可能不常体现，但在投资领域，我们始终在思考风险与幂律分布。我们之前谈到过，大多数投资都以失败告终，但少数成功案例足以抵消所有损失。在产品领域，我们也需要秉持同样的理念。若我负责的项目中有50%以失败告终，那将是个大问题。但这也激励我为公司持续布局，抓住可能改变业务轨迹的机遇。
